newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax group narrows gap on income tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: German tax group narrows gap on income tax cuts.

text.p: Germany's coalition tax commission has narrowed its differences on income tax cuts under a big reform package to take effect in 1999, commission sources said on Thursday.

Sources said the commission, headed by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, discussed on Wednesday cutting the lowest income tax rate to 19.5 percent from 26 percent and dropping the top rate to 37 or 38 percent from 53 percent.
But no final decisions were reached at the meeting, which was originally planned as the last. Four more sessions are planned before final proposals can be presented in January.

The proposed tax rates tend more towards a model favoured by Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU). Junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), have pressed for more dramatic cuts.

Sources said reform of corporation taxes, with separate rates for profits distributed to shareholders and retained earnings, was still undecided. Support is gaining ground to align corporation and income taxes, they said.
Waigel said on Wednesday progress had been made towards scrapping tax breaks to help offset most of the estimated 100 billion marks in lost revenues resulting from the cuts.
Travel allowances will be cut, among other measures, but it has not yet been agreed by how much.

An idea favoured by the CDU/CSU axis to increase value-added tax by two points to 17 percent to help pay for the tax reductions remained controversial. The smaller FDP, pinning its political survival on tax cuts, opposes such a move.
